verdict.reason: I cropped panel 2.3 of page-02.png at full resolution, and the problems the reviewer described are in the art. The top of Nagoji's balloon ("The king. If he is wise.") sits about 85 px higher at 300 DPI than the top of Ramayyan's question balloon. At about 7 mm in print, that is enough that some readers will take the answer before the question. The answer's tail is a long thin wedge. It starts at the balloon's left side near x 1030 and runs across the whole panel to the left frame edge, passing through Ramayyan's neck and shoulder, close to his face. A reader's eye goes from the balloon to Ramayyan, so the line reads as his, not as coming from the off-panel Nagoji. The balloon is also a narrow column with one or two words per line ("The / king. / If he / is / wise."), which is poor lettering. The script gives NAGOJI's answer after RAMAYYAN's question, so nothing in it allows this placement. The wording is right and the beat is present, so this is a localized lettering problem, not a blocker. The fix: a wider balloon placed after the question (lower and to the right), with a short tail off the left frame edge that does not cross Ramayyan.

refuted.description: The far-bank fort flies an orange/saffron pennant in 8.1, but the same Dutch bastion flies the red-white-blue banded flag in 8.3. A saffron pennant is the Maratha flag, reserved for memory panels. The fort's shape also changes from a large whitewashed fort with a domed turret (8.1) to a low bastion (8.3).
refuted.reason: Refuted after zooming in on page 8. The "orange pennant" in 8.1 is a tapered strip that the top panel border cuts off. It measures about 16 by 29 px on the 300 DPI page (original coordinates x 1472-1488, y 358-387), which is roughly 1.4 by 2.5 mm in print. At that size it reads as a speck of red-orange, not as a flag anyone could identify. No swallow tail is visible, so it does not match the bible's Maratha flag (a saffron swallow-tailed pennant, CONTINUITY.md line 191). The bible also allows plain, unlettered banners for other parties. The script asks for no fort or flag in 8.1 (lines 183-187). The Dutch bastion and its banded flag are required only in 8.3 (line 195), and 8.3 delivers them correctly: a plain red, white and blue flag with no monogram. The claimed change of fort shape is not supported either. The 8.1 fort and the 8.3 fort are both whitewashed curtain walls with a domed corner sentry turret, seen from different angles across the water. The 8.3 fort is a sizeable walled fort on a rock base, not a "low bastion". Ibrahim's line in 8.3 ("They can put forts on the banks") lets the backwaters hold more than one fort. A reader would see no flag conflict at print size.

refuted.description: Wrong speaker tail: Ramayyan's 'Watch instead.' balloon points into a stone pillar beside the sanctum door, not at Ramayyan.
refuted.reason: I checked page 2, panel 2.1 at full resolution. The tail of "Watch instead." does stop on the stone pillar, at about (1350, 587) in original pixels. But it points straight at Ramayyan. The tail runs from its base at about (1428, 515) to its tip at a slope of about (-78, +72). Extended along that line, it reaches about (1163, 760), which is Ramayyan's mouth and chin (his face spans about 1100-1180 x 640-760). Nothing else lies in that direction. The tail points away from the sanctum, and Nagoji is on the far left of the panel, so no reader would give the line to anyone but Ramayyan. Ramayyan also speaks the panel's other right-side balloon, "Who pays for the oil in those lamps?", and its tail clearly lands on his head, which reinforces the attribution. The script (2.1) gives both lines to Ramayyan, so the art matches it. In comic lettering a tail only needs to aim at the speaker, not touch him. The gap here is roughly 0.7 inch at 300 DPI, and the speaker is still unambiguous at print size. Lengthening the tail toward his mouth would be optional polish. It is not a wrong-speaker-tail error.

refuted.description: In the assassin inset, the palace behind the bowman is a European neoclassical stone mansion with cornices, urn finials and glazed arched fanlight windows. That style is wrong for a 1730s Travancore palace, which was timber and tiled like Padmanabhapuram, and it reads as 19th-century colonial.
refuted.reason: Refuted. I cropped and enlarged page 10, panel 10.1, inset 1 (x150-710, y1100-1390). The background building is stone, with moulded cornices and two small urn finials. But calling it "a European neoclassical mansion" that "reads as 19th-century colonial" overstates what is drawn. Its top is a hipped, pyramidal roof capped by a pot-shaped finial, which is closer to an Indian or Kerala roofline than to a pedimented neoclassical facade. The lit window near x660,y1240 is a tall pointed arch with fan tracery that passes as a jali or Indo-Islamic arch as easily as a Georgian fanlight. There is no balustrade or pediment I can make out. The roof the bowman crouches on is correctly drawn as Kerala-style tiles with a decorated ridge. The script only asks for "a bowman crouched on a palace roof" in a dark, desaturated tone, and it sets no rule for the palace's style. At print size (a 6.1 x 9.25 in page at 300 DPI), the inset is about 1.85 in wide, the building is under 1 in, and the window is about 0.1 in, all in near-black tones. At the one-third view of the whole page, the building reads only as a vague stone palace with a lit window. A reader will not see it as a colonial mansion, so this does not justify a redraw. If the author wants exact Padmanabhapuram timber gables, that is at most a minor polish note, not a major one.
